idiom_name: sealed wire hierarchy plus kotlinx.serialization class discriminator, exhaustive when to canonical
implementation_notes: kotlinx.serialization treats a sealed base type as closed polymorphism: it writes a class discriminator (default property name type, renameable with @JsonClassDiscriminator) and on decode selects the registered subclass, so the serializer is the router and each subclass's mapping is the per-format translator; @SerialName pins the discriminator value so renaming or moving a class cannot silently change the wire contract. The canonical form is a separate data class or value class - never the wire subclass - and the when over the decoded sealed type is exhaustive at compile time. For open or abstract hierarchies (formats contributed by another module) a SerializersModule with polymorphic {} and subclass() registers the translators explicitly, and hand-written function maps remain justified for non-JSON sources or heuristic detection.
pitfalls: The class discriminator defaults to the fully qualified class name and changes when a class moves or is renamed; set @SerialName on every wire-facing subclass.

Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true } is right for forward compatibility on the wire but wrong for the canonical target: unknown keys and missing required fields pass unnoticed if you decode straight into it.

coerceInputValues and explicitNulls decide whether a wrong-typed or null value becomes the property default - for a normalizer the strict setting is the honest one, because a coerced value is invisible data loss.

Closed polymorphism requires the subtypes and their serializers to be known in the same module; moving a format to another module turns the compile-time set into a runtime SerializersModule requirement.
